30		var everywhere bool
31		var allContexts bool
32		cmd := &cobra.Command{
33			Use:   "logout",
34			Short: "Log out of Entire",
35			Long: "Log out of Entire.\n\n" +
36				"By default this ends the active session only (server-side) and removes the\n" +

99	// logout cleared the previous one. This is what lets `entire logout` drain
100	// every login when run repeatedly: each call ends the active login and
101	// promotes the next, until none remain. Best-effort and informational —
102	// logout already succeeded by the time we get here.
103	func promoteNextLogin(outW, errW io.Writer) {
104		all, current, err := auth.Contexts()
105		if err != nil || current != "" || len(all) == 0 {
106			return
107		}

117	// bearer belongs to) — the default `entire logout`.
118	func revokeCurrentAuthSession(ctx context.Context, coreURL, token string) error {
119		return newAuthSessionsClient(coreURL, token).RevokeCurrentAuthSession(ctx) //nolint:wrapcheck // RevokeCurrentAuthSession already wraps with action context
120	}
121	
122	// revokeAllAuthSessions revokes every active login session on coreURL (the
123	// `entire logout --everywhere` path): list the families, then delete each by id.
124	// Best-effort across sessions — it attempts them all and returns the first
125	// failure, so one stuck session doesn't strand the rest.
126	func revokeAllAuthSessions(ctx context.Context, coreURL, token string) error {
127		client := newAuthSessionsClient(coreURL, token)
128		// ListAuthSessions and RevokeAuthSession already wrap with their own action
129		// context (incl. the session id), so return their errors verbatim.
130		sessions, err := client.ListAuthSessions(ctx)
131		if err != nil {
132			return err //nolint:wrapcheck // ListAuthSessions already wraps with "list sessions"
133		}
134		var firstErr error
135		for _, s := range sessions {
136			if err := client.RevokeAuthSession(ctx, s.ID); err != nil && firstErr == nil {
137				firstErr = err
138			}
139		}
140		return firstErr
141	}
142	
143	// runLogout ends the user's login. revoke is the caller-selected server-side
144	// revocation — just the active session, or every session on the active core
145	// when --everywhere is set. token is the resolved bearer for the revoke call
146	// (empty skips it). The active context (and its keyring entry) is removed
147	// either way, so the CLI reports logged-out even if the server call fails.
148	func runLogout(ctx context.Context, outW, errW io.Writer, token string, revoke boundRevokeFunc, clearContext clearContextFunc) error {
149		if token != "" {
150			if err := revoke(ctx); err != nil && !api.IsHTTPErrorStatus(err, http.StatusUnauthorized) {
151				// Best-effort: a transient network error shouldn't block local
152				// logout. A 401 means the token is already invalid server-side,
153				// so the desired state is achieved — no warning needed.
154				fmt.Fprintf(errW, "Warning: server-side session revocation failed: %v\n", err)
155			}
156		}
157	
158		if err := clearContext(); err != nil {
159			return fmt.Errorf("remove login: %w", err)
160		}
161	
162		fmt.Fprintln(outW, "Logged out.")
163		return nil
164	}
165	
166	// revokeTargetFunc revokes sessions on a specific core. The two production
167	// implementations are revokeCurrentAuthSession (just the bearer's own session)
168	// and revokeAllAuthSessions (every session on that core); `logout --all-contexts` picks
169	// one based on --everywhere and applies it to each saved context's core.
170	type revokeTargetFunc func(ctx context.Context, coreURL, token string) error
171	
172	// runLogoutAll drains every saved login. For each context it revokes the
173	// session(s) on that context's own core (using its own bearer) and removes
174	// the login locally. Per-context failures warn but never abort the sweep —
175	// one stuck login can't strand the rest, and local removal always proceeds
176	// so the CLI ends fully logged out.
177	//
178	// Dependencies are injected so the sweep is unit-testable without the real
179	// keyring or config dir: listContexts (auth.Contexts), tokenForContext
180	// (auth.LoginTokenForContext), revoke (revokeCurrentAuthSession/revokeAllAuthSessions),
181	// and removeContext (auth.RemoveContext).
182	func runLogoutAll(ctx context.Context, outW, errW io.Writer,
183		listContexts contextsProvider,
184		tokenForContext func(*contexts.Context) (string, error),
185		revoke revokeTargetFunc,
186		removeContext func(name string) error,
187		insecureHTTPAuth bool,
188	) error {
189		all, _, err := listContexts()
190		if err != nil {
191			return fmt.Errorf("list saved logins: %w", err)
192		}
193	
194		removed := 0
195		for _, c := range all {
196			token, terr := tokenForContext(c)
197			if terr != nil {
198				// Can't read this context's bearer — skip the server revoke but
199				// still drop it locally so it stops being reported as a login.
200				fmt.Fprintf(errW, "Warning: couldn't read token for %q; removing locally only: %v\n", c.Name, terr)
201				token = ""
202			}
203			if token != "" && c.CoreURL != "" && !insecureHTTPAuth {
204				if serr := api.RequireSecureURL(c.CoreURL); serr != nil {
205					// Never send a bearer over a non-TLS core; warn and skip the
206					// server revoke, but still remove the login locally.
207					fmt.Fprintf(errW, "Warning: skipping server-side revocation for %q: %v\n", c.Name, serr)
208					token = ""
209				}
210			}
211			if token != "" && c.CoreURL != "" {
212				if rerr := revoke(ctx, c.CoreURL, token); rerr != nil && !api.IsHTTPErrorStatus(rerr, http.StatusUnauthorized) {
213					fmt.Fprintf(errW, "Warning: server-side session revocation failed for %q: %v\n", c.Name, rerr)
214				}
215			}
216			if rerr := removeContext(c.Name); rerr != nil {
217				fmt.Fprintf(errW, "Warning: failed to remove saved login %q: %v\n", c.Name, rerr)
218				continue
219			}
220			removed++
221		}
222	
223		if removed == 0 {
224			fmt.Fprintln(outW, "No saved logins to remove.")
225		} else {
226			fmt.Fprintf(outW, "Logged out of %d saved login(s).\n", removed)
227		}
228		return nil
229	}

158	// Keychain, Credential Manager) can block indefinitely when no daemon
159	// is reachable, and an unbounded keyring call freezes the whole CLI.

174	}

177		_, err := callKeyringWithTimeout("delete", func() (string, error) {
178			return "", keyring.Delete(service, user)
179		})

181	}

**No — and that's a real gap for the persisted ones.**

There are two flavours of jurisdiction token, and only one is persisted:

**In-memory only (nothing to clean):** `entire auth token --jurisdiction` and `CellClientFactory` mint per-process and cache in a `mintSlot` (`cmd/entire/cli/auth/cell_data_api.go:133-137`, `212-256`). These die with the process.

**Persisted, and logout misses them:** `git-remote-entire` writes the jurisdiction token to the OS keychain under service `entire-jurisdiction:<audience>`, account = the context handle, so fresh git processes reuse it instead of paying the exchange per git command — `cmd/git-remote-entire/jurisdictionauth.go:39-43` and `:158`. Server-side TTL is 8h.

Logout only deletes two slots: `deleteContextKeychain(c.KeychainService, c.Handle)` removes `c.KeychainService` and `c.KeychainService+":refresh"` (`cmd/entire/cli/auth/context_store.go:69-80`) — i.e. `entire-core:<core-url>` and its refresh pair. The `entire-jurisdiction:*` prefix is never touched. The only code that deletes it is `jurisdictionTokenSource.Invalidate()`, wired to a data-plane 401 (`jurisdictionauth.go:174-185`).

So after `entire logout` (or `--everywhere` / `--all-contexts`), a bearer that authorizes git smart-HTTP against every repo the account can reach can survive in the keychain for up to 8h. Whether it still *works* depends on whether the core invalidates already-minted identity tokens when the login session is revoked — that's server-side and not decidable from this repo. If it doesn't, logout is leaving a live credential behind.

Fixing it needs a way to enumerate the audiences, which the CLI currently lacks: `tokenstore` has no list API, and `contexts.Context` (`internal/entireclient/contexts/contexts.go:31-44`) records only name/core/handle/keychain-service — no jurisdictions. Two workable shapes:

1. Record minted audiences on the context entry (a `jurisdiction_audiences` field written where `jurisdictionauth.go:158` persists), then have `deleteContextKeychain` delete each `entire-jurisdiction:<aud>` slot. Offline, exact.
2. Derive audiences from the cluster catalog at logout time and delete each slot. No schema change, but adds a network call to logout and silently misses anything the catalog no longer lists.

I'd go with (1) — logout must not depend on the network to be complete. Want me to write it up as an issue, or implement it?
Ok, lets go with 1.  I'm on a branch.

10	// the login JWT) so fresh git-remote-entire processes reuse it instead of
11	// paying the exchange per git command — with the server-side 8h

14	// runners are ephemeral — and memoizes in-process only.

33	// rotates the jurisdiction token before actual expiry. One minute covers clock
34	// skew and gives slow downstream RPCs a fresh token. Matches
35	// admincreds.safetyMargin so the cred caches don't diverge on freshness
36	// semantics.
37	const tokenSafetyMargin = time.Minute
38	
39	// jurisdictionKeyringService is the keychain service name for jurisdiction
40	// tokens, keyed by audience so tokens for different jurisdictions
41	// (and prod vs staging) can't be confused. The account is the context handle.
42	func jurisdictionKeyringService(audience string) string {

47	// authenticates every git request: one token covers every repo the account
48	// can reach. Tokens come from, in order: the in-process memo, the OS
49	// keychain (interactive path only), or a fresh /oauth/token exchange.
50	type jurisdictionTokenSource struct {

52		// common case where the cluster's jurisdiction is the login's home.
53		homeCoreURL string
54		// audience is the cluster's advertised jurisdiction audience.
55		audience string

57		// audience — the cross-jurisdiction exchange endpoint. It rides the
58		// same TLS-authenticated /.well-known trust root as the audience.
59		jurisdictionCoreURL string

61		// home/cross-jurisdiction routing (which needs a home_jurisdiction claim
62		// the ENTIRE_TOKEN path's sa-session JWTs don't carry). Set by
63		// newEnvJurisdictionTokenSource to the env token's own trust-gated core.
64		fixedCoreURL string

66		// resolver sets it when it can already see why the exchange is doomed
67		// (an ENTIRE_TOKEN from a different jurisdiction than the cluster's),

122		}

124		if s.persist {

127				// decodes to a valid timestamp but no token — otherwise it would
128				// produce bare "Bearer " headers until the entry expired.
129				//

133				// SafetyMargin before actual expiry — individual git requests are

221	// audience and no routing is needed. Otherwise: the login's own core when
222	// the audience is in the login's home jurisdiction, else the cluster's
223	// advertised jurisdiction core. The home core is the issuer the user logged
224	// in at, used verbatim (it may legitimately be loopback http in local dev);

226	// must be https before the login JWT is POSTed to it.
227	func (s *jurisdictionTokenSource) exchangeCore(loginJWT string) (string, error) {

230		}

233		if err != nil {

235		}

238			return "", fmt.Errorf("read home jurisdiction: %w", err)
239		}
240		if home == "" {

242		}
243		// jurisdictionLabel lowercases the audience host; fold the claim too so
244		// the comparison doesn't hinge on core config region keys being lowercase.
245		if strings.ToLower(home) == label {

248	
249		if s.jurisdictionCoreURL == "" {
250			return "", fmt.Errorf("cross-jurisdiction token exchange for %s: cluster advertises no jurisdiction_core_url", s.audience)
251		}
252		if !strings.HasPrefix(s.jurisdictionCoreURL, "https://") {
253			return "", fmt.Errorf("advertised jurisdiction core %q must be https", s.jurisdictionCoreURL)
254		}
255		return s.jurisdictionCoreURL, nil
256	}

258	// jurisdictionLabel extracts the jurisdiction label from an audience like
259	// https://au.entire.io ("au"), for comparison against the login JWT's
260	// home_jurisdiction claim.

262		u, err := url.Parse(audience)

268		if !ok || label == "" || rest == "" {
269			return "", fmt.Errorf("jurisdiction audience %q has no <jurisdiction>.<domain> host", audience)
270		}
271		return label, nil
272	}

### Jurisdiction Token Cleanup on Logout

Jurisdiction (data-plane) access tokens come in two flavours, and only one is
persisted. `entire auth token --jurisdiction` and `CellClientFactory` mint
in-process and die with the process. `git-remote-entire` instead caches its
token in the credential store at `tokenstore.JurisdictionService(audience)`
(`entire-jurisdiction:<audience>`, keyed by the context handle) so a fresh
helper process per git command doesn't re-run the exchange.

That cached token is a bearer for every repo the account can reach, with an 8h
server-side TTL that outlives the login JWT — so **logout must delete it**, and
the credential store has no enumeration API to find it with. The bookkeeping
that closes that loop:

- `contexts.Context.JurisdictionAudiences` records which audiences a context has
  a token filed for. Anything a *writer* persists must appear here first.
- `auth.RememberJurisdictionAudience(name, audience)` appends it (idempotent,
  trailing-slash-trimmed). `jurisdictionTokenSource.persistToken` calls it
  **before** `tokenstore.Set`, and skips the write entirely when it fails — an
  unrecorded persisted token is invisible to logout, whereas a skipped write
  only costs one exchange.
- `deleteContextKeychain` (`auth/context_store.go`) deletes refresh → every
  recorded jurisdiction slot → access, longest-lived first, and treats any
  non-`ErrNotFound` failure as a logout failure.
- `RecordLoginContext` carries the list across the re-login upsert: the tokens
  are keyed by audience + handle, not by login session, so they survive a fresh
  login and must stay findable.

Any new writer of a per-jurisdiction credential must follow the same
record-then-write order, or logout will leave a live credential behind.

### Jurisdiction Token Cleanup on Logout

Jurisdiction (data-plane) access tokens come in two flavours, and only one is
persisted. `entire auth token --jurisdiction` and `CellClientFactory` mint
in-process and die with the process. `git-remote-entire` instead caches its
token in the credential store at `tokenstore.JurisdictionService(audience)`
(`entire-jurisdiction:<audience>`, keyed by the context handle) so a fresh
helper process per git command doesn't re-run the exchange.

That cached token is a bearer for every repo the account can reach, with an 8h
server-side TTL that outlives the login JWT — so **logout must delete it**, and
the credential store has no enumeration API to find it with. The bookkeeping
that closes that loop:

- `contexts.Context.JurisdictionAudiences` records which audiences a context has
  a token filed for. Anything a *writer* persists must appear here first.
- `auth.RememberJurisdictionAudience(name, audience)` appends it (idempotent,
  trailing-slash-trimmed). `jurisdictionTokenSource.persistToken` calls it
  **before** `tokenstore.Set`, and skips the write entirely when it fails — an
  unrecorded persisted token is invisible to logout, whereas a skipped write
  only costs one exchange.
- `deleteContextKeychain` (`auth/context_store.go`) deletes refresh → every
  recorded jurisdiction slot → access, longest-lived first, and treats any
  non-`ErrNotFound` failure as a logout failure.
- `RecordLoginContext` carries the list across the re-login upsert: the tokens
  are keyed by audience + handle, not by login session, so they survive a fresh
  login and must stay findable.

Any new writer of a per-jurisdiction credential must follow the same
record-then-write order, or logout will leave a live credential behind.

Do you understand what a jurisdiction token is?  I'm wondering if we should also remove them when changing contexts ("entire auth use ..." or "entire auth login ...").  They seem to be stored scoped to a target region, rather than by the context, so an "entire auth use ..." may not actually swap them.

Yes. A jurisdiction token is what `git-remote-entire` puts in the `Authorization` header for git smart-HTTP: an RFC 8693 exchange of the login JWT, `scope=openid`, `aud` = the cluster's advertised `jurisdiction_audience`. It names the *account*, not a repo — the data plane authorizes each request live against regional SpiceDB — so one token covers every repo that account can reach in that jurisdiction, for the full 8h server TTL, independent of the login session.

Your read of the storage is right, and the distinction matters: the slot is `(entire-jurisdiction:<audience>, handle)` — scoped by region **and account**, but not by context. Account-scoped is what carries most of the weight:

- **`auth use` between two different accounts** — different handles, different slots. No crossover today. Deleting on switch would only force a re-exchange on the next git command; it buys nothing.
- **`auth login`, re-login as the same identity** — legitimately reuses the cached token. What makes it valid is the 8h TTL and live SpiceDB authz, not the login session, so a fresh login has nothing to invalidate.
- **prod vs staging** — different audience hosts (`eu.entire.io` vs `eu.partial.to`), so no sharing.

Where it genuinely breaks is the case you're circling, but it isn't switch-time. Contexts are keyed by (core URL, handle), so **two contexts can share a handle across two cores** — and a cluster advertises multiple trusted cores with a single `jurisdiction_audience`, so both contexts hash to one slot. Whoever mints first wins, and the other identity reads that token.

That can happen with no `auth use` at all: `selectContext` (`internal/entireclient/clusterdiscovery/resolve.go:227`) picks a context **per cluster** — active context if eligible, else the sole eligible one. So cluster A can be using context X while cluster B uses context Y, in the same instant, from the same machine. A hook on `auth use` / `login` never sees that path.

So I'd not add deletion to `use`/`login`. The structural fix is to make the slot key context-scoped — the account key becomes something like `alice@core.eu.entire.io` (handle + core host) instead of bare `alice`, both in `jurisdictionauth.go` and in `deleteContextKeychain`, both derived from the context so no new bookkeeping. Then two contexts can never share a slot, switching needs no cleanup, and logout's recorded-audience sweep becomes exact rather than "exact as long as handles don't collide."

Two wrinkles if we do it: existing `entire-jurisdiction:*` entries keyed by bare handle become unreachable — one extra exchange per audience after upgrade (harmless), but also undeletable by logout, so I'd have `deleteContextKeychain` delete both spellings for a release before dropping the old one.

Worth noting the ambiguity I can't settle from this repo: whether a handle is globally unique across cores in one deployment. If it is, the collision is unreachable today and the key change is hardening rather than a bug fix. Either way it's cheap.

git commit -F - <<'EOF'
fix(auth): delete jurisdiction tokens on logout

`git-remote-entire` caches its jurisdiction (data-plane) access token in the
credential store at `entire-jurisdiction:<audience>`, keyed by the context
handle, so a fresh helper process per git command doesn't re-run the RFC 8693
exchange. Logout deleted only the `entire-core:<core>` access + refresh slots,
so that token — a bearer for every repo the account can reach in its
jurisdiction, with an 8h server-side TTL — survived `entire logout`,
`--everywhere` and `--all-contexts` alike.

The credential store has no enumeration API and the audience isn't derivable
offline, so track it: `contexts.Context.JurisdictionAudiences` records the
audiences a context has a token filed for, and `deleteContextKeychain` walks
that list. Deletion order is longest-lived-first (refresh, jurisdiction,
access) so a mid-sequence failure leaves behind only the shorter-lived
credential, and a failed delete still aborts the logout rather than reporting
success over a surviving credential.

`jurisdictionTokenSource.persistToken` records the audience *before* writing
the token, and skips the write when recording fails: a persisted-but-unrecorded
token is invisible to logout, whereas skipping costs one exchange. The recorder
being non-nil now also selects the persisted flavour, replacing the `persist`
flag, so the two can't disagree — the ENTIRE_TOKEN path passes none and stays
in-process-only. `RecordLoginContext` carries the audience list across the
re-login upsert, since the tokens are keyed by audience + handle rather than by
login session and outlive a fresh login.

Deletion is scoped to the outgoing context: only its recorded audiences, only
under its own handle, so another account's tokens are untouched. Slots written
before this bookkeeping are unreachable and expire with their TTL.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>
EOF
